author: Julius Njogu
title: Regulars Say This Historic California Restaurant Serves Fried Chicken Just Like Grandma Used to Make - NewsBreak
text:
By Julius Njogu ,
9 hours ago Some restaurants win people over with trendy menus and elaborate presentations. Others keep customers coming back with something much simpler: crispy fried chicken, warm biscuits, homemade-style sides, and a slice of pie that reminds them of childhood.
That old-fashioned charm is exactly what makes Mrs. Knott’s Chicken Dinner Restaurant in Buena Park, California, such a memorable dining destination.
Just outside Knott’s Berry Farm, this historic restaurant has served comforting American classics since 1934. What began as a small family business during the Great Depression eventually helped create one of Southern California’s best-known amusement parks.
More than 90 years later, the restaurant continues serving fried chicken based on founder Cordelia Knott’s original recipes. For many longtime customers, the attraction is not just the food. It is the feeling of returning to a familiar family tradition.
A Humble Chicken Dinner That Helped Build a Theme Park Image credit: serezniy/123rf Long before roller coasters became the main attraction, the Knott family was selling berries, preserves, and homemade food along Beach Boulevard.
During the Great Depression, Walter and Cordelia Knott needed another way to support their growing family. Cordelia believed her fried chicken could attract customers, so she added it to the family’s small tea room.
On June 13, 1934, she served her first eight chicken dinners.
Each meal cost just 65 cents, and Cordelia presented the food on her own wedding china. It was a modest beginning, but customers quickly took notice.
According to Knott’s Berry Farm’s history , the restaurant grew from four tables to 20 by the end of 1934. By 1936, its seating capacity had grown to 70.
Eventually, the crowds became so large that Walter Knott began developing an Old West attraction to entertain people waiting for dinner.
That attraction grew into the Ghost Town area and helped establish Knott’s Berry Farm as a theme park.
Think about that for a moment. One woman’s fried chicken became a driving force behind an entire amusement park.
The restaurant’s popularity has continued across generations. During its 90th anniversary celebration in 2024, Knott’s reported that the establishment had served more than 90 million pounds of chicken throughout its history.
The Fried Chicken Still Follows Cordelia’s Original Recipe Of course, history alone cannot keep a restaurant busy for nine decades. Eventually, the food has to deliver.
At Mrs. Knott’s, fried chicken remains the menu’s star.
The restaurant continues using recipes associated with Cordelia Knott, preserving the traditional cooking style that made its early dinners famous.
In a 2024 interview with CBS Los Angeles, Knott’s Berry Farm executive chef Bobby Obezo explained that the kitchen still follows Cordelia’s recipe, including the breading and double-frying process.
The goal is straightforward: golden chicken with a flavorful coating and a satisfying, old-fashioned character.
The restaurant’s complete chicken dinner includes four pieces of fried chicken with several classic sides.
This isn’t one of those dinners where the main course arrives beside a lonely spoonful of vegetables.
The meal comes with biscuits, soup, salad or rhubarb selections, mashed potatoes, a vegetable side, and dessert.
It is the kind of spread that encourages diners to settle in rather than rush through dinner.
Customer reviews are not universally glowing. Some visitors praise the traditional flavor and filling portions, while others find the seasoning or sides relatively simple.
That distinction matters. Mrs. Knott’s is not trying to reinvent fried chicken with unusual sauces or elaborate toppings. Its reputation rests on delivering a familiar country-style meal.
For customers seeking nostalgia rather than culinary experimentation, that simplicity is part of the appeal.
The Biscuits, Rhubarb, and Boysenberry Pie Complete the Experience Fried chicken may bring customers through the door, but the accompanying dishes help explain why this restaurant has become a family tradition.
Start with the biscuits.
These soft, handmade favorites are a signature part of the meal, particularly when paired with the restaurant’s boysenberry preserves.
Then comes a side that might surprise first-time visitors: rhubarb.
Rhubarb was included in Cordelia Knott’s original chicken dinners , alongside mashed potatoes, salad, biscuits, and pie.
It remains associated with the restaurant’s traditional menu today, including a cherry-rhubarb preparation.
For diners accustomed to choosing between ordinary side salads and vegetables, the sweet-tart flavor offers something different.
The mashed potatoes with gravy deliver another familiar country-dinner favorite. Guests can also choose vegetables such as corn or cabbage, depending on their meal selection.
But perhaps the most memorable finish is dessert.
The classic dinner includes boysenberry or apple pie.
Boysenberries have deep roots in Knott’s history. Walter Knott helped develop the fruit commercially, and the family’s berry products became closely associated with their roadside business.
The boysenberry pie therefore carries a little extra significance. It connects today’s customers with the farming operation that existed before the restaurant and amusement park became famous.
For first-time visitors, choosing boysenberry pie seems especially fitting.
After all, how often can dessert tell part of a restaurant’s origin story?
A Farmhouse Atmosphere That Keeps the Past Alive Food is only part of the restaurant’s personality.
Inside, Mrs. Knott’s maintains a country-inspired atmosphere that reflects its beginnings as a family tea room.
Different dining areas celebrate different parts of the restaurant’s history.
The Tea Room draws inspiration from the original dining space that welcomed guests in 1934. Its booths and windows connect to the restaurant’s earliest years.
Another room, called the Pantry, takes inspiration from Cordelia Knott’s kitchen. Rustic furnishings and a potbelly stove help create the impression of an old-fashioned farmhouse gathering space.
The barn-inspired dining room continues the country theme, while the restaurant also offers patio seating overlooking the California Marketplace fountain.
For those looking for something beyond the traditional dining rooms, a full-service bar offers boysenberry-inspired drinks.
The overall setting makes the restaurant suitable for family celebrations, casual lunches, and relaxed dinners after visiting nearby attractions.
Its long history also attracts customers who remember eating there decades ago.
In a 2024 CBS Los Angeles report, longtime visitor Ruth James recalled the area before the amusement park developed into what visitors recognize today.
Stories like hers help explain why Mrs. Knott’s means more to some families than an ordinary restaurant.
It is a place where childhood memories and present-day outings can meet around the same dinner table.
Why This Old-Fashioned Chicken Dinner Still Matters California has no shortage of restaurants offering fried chicken. What makes Mrs. Knott’s different is the history surrounding every plate.
Few dining establishments can trace their beginnings to eight Depression-era dinners served on wedding china and connect that story to the creation of a major amusement park.
The menu still celebrates the foods that made Cordelia Knott’s kitchen famous: fried chicken, biscuits, traditional vegetables, rhubarb, and berry pie.
Not every diner will consider it the best fried chicken they have ever tasted. Preferences vary, and the restaurant’s straightforward cooking style may not appeal to everyone.
Still, there is something special about enjoying a meal that connects generations of California families.
For visitors who appreciate generous country-style dinners, a little nostalgia, and a slice of local history, Mrs. Knott’s Chicken Dinner Restaurant offers an experience that goes well beyond the plate.
And if the meal reminds someone of Sunday dinner at Grandma’s house, that might be the highest compliment an old-fashioned restaurant could receive.
